answer.rationale: The 18% cost-cut mandate is the binding constraint, but the assembly line is running at 94% with no buffer, so any disruption to delivery is unacceptable. That rules out switch_primary_vendor (onboarding risk, even if past onboarding was quick, a 14-day window with no buffer is too tight) and defer_decision (the contract does not auto-renew in 14 days, so inaction means losing supply). add_second_source would reduce single-point-of-failure risk but would not by itself deliver the 18% cut and would add cost in the near term, working against the finance mandate. The memory record (c4) shows that negotiating at renewal has previously recovered real margin on both price and payment terms, and (c1) shows that renewing with the incumbent preserves integration stability and delivery continuity. c6 further suggests that pairing renewal with a longer-term commitment can unlock volume pricing. Therefore the single highest-leverage action within the 14-day window is to negotiate_terms with the incumbent at renewal: seek price concessions and payment-term improvements sized to absorb the 18% cut, potentially offering a multi-year commitment in exchange, while keeping the existing integration and delivery schedule intact. If negotiation fails to close the gap, the fallback (next cycle) would be add_second_source to create competitive pressure and redundancy.
